answers.question: I want to be ready for the 5K in November. Should I run every day next week to get there faster?
answers.answer: No, running every day would not get you there faster. Three runs a week, with a rest day between them, lets your body adapt and gives you the best chance of running the whole 5K in November. Keep the walk breaks in your runs, and shorten them gradually. Each week you will be able to run a little longer before you need to walk.

new.analysis:
Last week was a steady first week. You ran three times, covered 6.78 km in about an hour, reported no pain, and your heart rate stayed mostly in the easy zone. The calf tightness you noted is the one thing to watch, but it cleared by the next morning each time, so I am treating it as normal early load for now.

Running every day would add load faster than your calves and tendons can adapt. Your heart and lungs adjust quickly, but the muscles and tendons in the lower leg take longer, and rest days are when they catch up. Three runs with a rest day between each one will do more for your 5K than a fourth or fifth run would.

This week's total is about 68 minutes, roughly 6 percent more than last week. The longest run goes from 24 to 28 minutes. That is a small step, which is how volume should grow from a low base.

This is the build phase, but for a new runner the harder work is running for longer, not running faster. So there is no speed work or threshold running yet, and I have left out the strides because of the calves. If the calves settle over the next week, I will add short strides in the week of Sep 7. The Saturday run is the one session with more effort in it, and the two shorter runs stay easy.

Over the coming weeks, the walk breaks should get shorter, one step at a time. My aim is continuous running for about 30 minutes by mid October, which leaves time to build toward the full 5 km. I will plan a lighter week in the week of Sep 21 so the load does not climb without a break.
